1039.title: Raised lower bounds for 56 square counts, including s(112) ≥ 10.782475680330
1039.body:
**Credit name.** Joost de Winter, Delft University of Technology, after Hiroaki Hosono.

**Claim.** I am submitting lower bounds for 56 square counts between 19 and 148. There are 49 direct results and seven consequences of monotonicity. The largest increase over the strongest earlier comparison in the packet is at 112, from 10.750737071037 to 10.782475680330. SquareMath's best listed lower bound there was 10.711734195583. The table below uses downward-rounded decimals. The attachment supplies the exact rational or square root of a rational for every row.

**Certificate.** Attached file `lower-bounds-56.zip`, source commit `e94e6ce65a887f80dd4821454df53c0c18a4ba97`, archive SHA-256 `9641ca15ac63213db22ad32854efb0bc0575d7c0beeb646fd6931f50ae183452`. The attachment is self-contained. `exact_claims.csv` maps all 56 claims to their proof and exact inputs. The `.source/` directory contains the raw Git commit object contents. The included verifier authenticates the source tree against that commit. The registry comparison uses jlevy/squares at `1015fc175fa4e2c01f912d915d784100e36d3bab`.

**Argument.** Each direct proof starts with a nonnegative measure of total mass strictly below the square count. The angular cover and center-domain checks ensure a suitable core inside every admissible square captures mass at least one. The proofs address disjointness of cores and boundary mass for the type of measure used. This rules out packing the claimed count in any smaller board. A packing for a larger count contains a packing for a smaller count, which gives the seven corollaries.

**Checking.** Extract the attachment and run `python3 verify.py` using Python 3.10+ and a C++17 compiler with 128-bit integers. The verifier recomputes the 56 exact claims, checks every decimal against its exact value, checks the mass budgets and archived direction receipts, and reconstructs the 82- and 112-square measures. On the handoff machine this takes under one minute. For examples of fresh native center checks, run `python3 rectangles/replay.py hybrid_n109_main 570` and `python3 mixed/replay.py n101_r400_s12_proj 200`. Both passed on preparation. Instructions for larger replays are in the README.

**Shared premises and review scope.** The methods share source measures, square symmetries and the mass-counting argument. Some claims use original coverage, some combine old and new directions, and others have complete integer-checked direction sets from the search. The coverage column identifies the history for each proof. The handoff rechecked every transfer against the retained evidence and reran selected native direction checks. Independent project review, a full fresh replay of all historical directions, and formalization remain open.

**Lineage and AI assistance.** Hiroaki Hosono constructed the source measures. The 109-square work builds on my T-327 rescaling of his 108-square measure. The attached evidence identifies inherited inputs separately from changed mass distributions, additional center and angle checks, and new transfers. GPT6.2 Astra helped develop the constructions, perform the computations, and prepare the certificates and this report.

1041.title: Raised lower bounds for 34 square counts, including s(114) ≥ 87/8 = 10.875 (follow-up to #1039)
1041.body:
[squaremath_continued_20261119.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/35084690/squaremath_continued_20261119.zip)

**Credit name.** Joost de Winter, Delft University of Technology, after Hiroaki Hosono.

**Claim.** Lower bounds for 34 square counts between 50 and 137, each a direct certificate with its own complete coverage check. The largest increase is at 114, from 10.807801610697 (#1039) to 87/8 = 10.875. The case page lists the upper bound 11 there, so the gap shrinks from 0.19 to 0.125. Every bound is an exact rational, listed in `lower_bounds.csv` and in the table below.

**Certificate.** Attached file `squaremath_continued_20261119.zip`, SHA-256 `d8d0d6966f7ac7f9a69f24d578619ee2323a158e5c6c9c7e6be9039c401445df`. Comparisons use jlevy/squares at `1015fc175fa4e2c01f912d915d784100e36d3bab` and the bounds submitted in #1039.

**Argument.** Each certificate places a nonnegative rectangle measure on the board of the claimed side, with total mass strictly below the square count. The checker proves that every unit square in the board, at every orientation and centre, captures mass at least one. For an angle interval with half-width σ around orientation θ₀, the octagon |u| + σ|v| ≤ 1/2, |v| + σ|u| ≤ 1/2 lies in every unit square of that interval, and the checker moves this octagon through all permitted centres with integer area bounds. Square boundaries carry no mass, so a packing would need more mass than the measure holds. Details are in `proof/INTEGER_CHECKER.md`.

**Constructions.** The measures come from Hosono's measures and from the reweighted measures of #1039. Two steps are new. A strip step repeats the central unit strip of a measure on each axis, which raises the board side by two (the 73-square measure at 8.826 gives a 114-square measure at 10.826). A mixture step combines measures transplanted from several counts with integer weights. The bound at 114 mixes measures from 92, 93 and 74 squares with weights 9184590 : 73911664 : 16903746. All mixtures and weights are listed in `constructions/README.md` and rebuilt with rational arithmetic.

**Checking.** Run `python3 verify.py` (Python 3.10+, C++17 compiler with 128-bit integers). It checks all input hashes, rebuilds every measure, and checks the recorded coverage of all angle intervals. `python3 verify.py --replay --workers 4` repeats every centre subdivision, with negative controls at quarter-strength weights. `python3 verify.py --n 114 --replay --workers 4` replays the bound at 114 alone (100 angle intervals, 1,406,930 centre boxes). Both the full check and the replay at 114 passed on a separate machine.

**Not claimed here.** The packet also holds 67 bounds from new corner measures (`corners/`) that inherit the global coverage of Hosono's T-180 measures without replaying it, and a packing of 260 squares that differs from earlier certificates by 1.6e-15. This issue claims neither.

**Lineage and AI assistance.** Hiroaki Hosono constructed the source measures. The reweighted measures and the integer checker come from my earlier submissions, #1039 and T-327. OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra carried out the numerical search, the derivations and the certificate construction under my direction.

1042.title: Raised lower bounds for 48 square counts between 50 and 218, including s(136) ≥ 11.868
1042.body:
**Credit name.** Joost de Winter, Delft University of Technology, after Hiroaki Hosono.

**Claim.** Lower bounds for 48 square counts between 50 and 218. Every bound is an exact rational with its own coverage proof. The largest gains are at 136 (11.6915 → 11.868), 137 (→ 11.8813), 188 (→ 13.858) and 161 (12.8 → 12.858). The table lists all 48 with the previous value, its source and the method.

**Certificate.** Folder `lower_bounds_2026_11_19` of https://github.com/JoostdeWinter/square-packing at commit 21d944c43098e2261ab7d713cd10f02a5eb13f3d. `CLAIM.md` lists the claimed bounds. Exact values and proof types are in `followup/best_by_count.csv`.

**Argument.** Each certificate places a nonnegative rectangle measure on the board of the claimed side, with total mass strictly below the square count. The checker proves that every unit square in the board, at every orientation and centre, captures mass at least one. Square boundaries carry no mass, so a packing would need more mass than the measure holds. The coverage check is described in `proof/INTEGER_CHECKER.md`.

**Methods.** Most bounds are standalone certificates built from Hosono's measures and the measures of #1039, partly as integer-weighted mixtures of measures from several counts (`constructions/README.md`). Three further methods are new:
- Repeated central strips (`followup/repeated`). A unit square projects to an interval of width at most √2 on each axis, so a measure whose three central unit strips are identical keeps its coverage when more such strips are inserted. One proof then covers several board sizes. This gives 188, 189 and 218.
- Four translated regions (`followup/envelopes`): an upper bound on the combined mass of four overlapping regions of an earlier certificate, used at 137, 138 and 162.
- Reduced corner mass on a periodic board (`followup/corner_trim`), used at 217. Only unit squares that can meet a changed corner receive a second coverage check.

**Checking.** Run `python3 followup/verify.py` in the folder (Python 3.10+). It rebuilds the measures, checks the recorded coverage and the strip, region and corner arguments. A full replay of the centre subdivisions needs a C++17 compiler: `python3 followup/verify.py --n 114 --replay --workers 4` replays a single count. `followup/native-audits.json` records 15 full and 9 sampled native replays, each with a separate rational polygon check.

**Not claimed.** The folder also holds 67 corner bounds that inherit the global coverage of Hosono's T-180 measures, 16 edge-strip refinements of #1039 with gains near 1e-11, and precision refinements of existing packings. This issue claims none of them.

**Lineage and AI authorship.** Hiroaki Hosono constructed the source measures. The reweighted measures and the integer checker come from my earlier submissions, #1039 and T-327. GPT6.2 Astra was the AI author for the numerical search, derivations and certificate construction under my direction.

**Follow-up registration for 161 squares.** I obtain $s(161)\ge8036307/625000=12.8580912$, an exact increase of $57/625000=0.0000912$ over the $12.858$ in this issue.

The source is the 363-interval certificate at side $12.858$ previously used for the 188-square construction. On the new board, I split the possible centers at $q=18553/5000$ on both axes and use the existing four-region transfer. Every admissible unit square captures mass at least one. Outward-rounded integer integration gives total mass at most $4024992052429083498016487/25000000000000000000000=160.99968209716333992065948<161$. A second integer sweep gives the same numerator. The original 217-square claim still uses its own anchor at $1607/125$.

Everything needed to reproduce this follow-up is already in the [pinned proof package](https://github.com/JoostdeWinter/square-packing/tree/21d944c43098e2261ab7d713cd10f02a5eb13f3d/lower_bounds_2026_11_19). From the `lower_bounds_2026_11_19` folder, run the following with Python 3.10 or later.

```python
from pathlib import Path
import gzip, json, sys
sys.path.insert(0, 'followup/envelopes')
from envelope_exact import verify

p = Path('followup/repeated/161--749858-12.858-100-uniform/proof')
measure = json.loads(gzip.decompress((p / 'k100.json.gz').read_bytes()))
verify(measure, [{
    'n': 161, 'side': '8036307/625000', 'seam': '18553/5000',
    'mass': '4024992052429083498016487/25000000000000000000000',
    'previous_upper_endpoint': '6429/500',
    'grid_sha256': '77dc67536419e9b775304747ca446308810663e6d3b23a9a428c49a38149778b',
}])
```

The source replay passed all 363 orientation checks and three negative controls, and four rational polygon integrations also passed. To repeat the native checks, run `python3 proof/replay.py followup/repeated/161--749858-12.858-100-uniform/proof --controls --workers 4`.

The source measures descend from Hiroaki Hosono’s work. GPT6.2 Astra was the AI author for the seam search and proof checks under my direction.
